question: access

request.from: a cloud container in a datacenter network, one IP
request.body: Four keyless GETs of the protected-resource document: at the root path the challenge names, at the RFC 9728 path-inserted path for the real endpoint, at a path invented for this pass, and on the second hostname the challenge names. Then the authorization-server metadata on both hostnames.

decoded.four-identical-documents: All four returned 200 with 270 bytes and ONE sha256, 6b80dbdbb15f3a35b4b90e2eb7f96ffbc7ccdec9c3b218b333476c460a2e07a1: mcp.figma.com root at 12:19:52.653Z, mcp.figma.com/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource/mcp at 12:19:51.456Z, mcp.figma.com/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource/bogus-f0c8bfeb at 12:19:56.123Z, and api.figma.com root at 12:20:25.900Z.
decoded.document: resource https://mcp.figma.com/mcp; authorization_servers [https://api.figma.com]; bearer_methods_supported [header]; scopes_supported [mcp:connect]; resource_name Figma MCP; resource_documentation https://developers.figma.com/docs/figma-mcp-server/
decoded.the-invented-path: The third URL was invented for this pass and names no resource of this vendor. It answered 200 with a document declaring a DIFFERENT resource. So on this host the presence of a protected-resource document is not evidence that the path it was requested under is a resource. Nothing is misrepresented about the server that does exist, and this is not offered as a security finding.
decoded.comparison: Measured the same hour on mcp.asana.com, the equivalent invented path (/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource/v2/mcp/bogus-f0c8bfeb) answered 404 with a 9-byte body. The two hosts differ in exactly this respect, and a sweep that reads only status codes would score them the same.
decoded.authorization-server: GET /.well-known/oauth-authorization-server at 12:19:54.349Z on mcp.figma.com and at 12:20:25.150Z on api.figma.com: both 200, 701 bytes, one sha256 ff45329c0e296560957a34ec2768516c377d16f2dcd1cae3f546b92bcd2f8c45. issuer https://api.figma.com; registration_endpoint https://api.figma.com/v1/oauth/mcp/register; NO client-ID metadata document; code_challenge_methods_supported [S256]; token_endpoint_auth_methods_supported [client_secret_basic, client_secret_post] with no none; require_state_parameter true; authorization_response_iss_parameter_supported true; grant_types_supported includes urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:jwt-bearer; authorization_grant_profiles_supported [urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-profile:id-jag].
decoded.openid-configuration: 404 at 32 bytes on the resource host, so the two well-known documents are not aliases here as they are at most vendors this registry has read.
decoded.vendor-words: The vendor's own documentation names what the jwt-bearer grant and the id-jag profile are for. Asked 'Does the MCP server support enterprise-managed authorization?', the Rate limits & access page answers 'Yes, for Claude through Okta Cross App Access (XAA).'
decoded.not-measured: whether the registration endpoint registers a client (a POST there is a write and was not made), and any token request

finding: The protected-resource document on mcp.figma.com is served for every path under its well-known prefix, including one invented for this pass, and byte-identically on api.figma.com: four URLs, 200, 270 bytes, one sha256, all declaring the resource as https://mcp.figma.com/mcp. On this host, therefore, a 200 from that prefix is not evidence that the requested path is a resource. The authorization server is the same document on both hostnames, issuer api.figma.com, advertising dynamic client registration and no client-ID metadata document, S256 only, and the jwt-bearer grant with the identity-assertion profile the vendor says it uses for Okta Cross App Access.

reproducibility.command: for p in '' /mcp /bogus-f0c8bfeb; do curl -sS -D- "https://mcp.figma.com/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource$p"; done; curl -sS -D- https://api.figma.com/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource; curl -sS -D- https://api.figma.com/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server
